newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norway's next premier mulls his government.
newsitem.headline: Norway's next premier mulls his government.

text.p: Norway's next prime minister Thorbjoern Jagland spent Thursday, the day before he takes office, putting together the government that will succeed the cabinet led by Gro Harlem Brundtland.

Jagland and his aides met to set up the new Labour Party administration following Brundtland's surprise announcement on Wednesday that she was resigning to give the party a fresh start for next year's elections.
"I will contact those I want in my government," Jagland told the daily Aftenposten.
Brundtland, 57, who dominated Norwegian politics for 15 years, will formally resign on Friday with her 18-member government, including seven women, at a regular cabinet meeting at the Royal Palace.
Another meeting will follow at which 46-year-old Jagland, who as party leader has been groomed four years to become premier, will take over and present his government.

Brundtland said she was quitting before a Labour Party congress next month so that the party, which forms a minority government, could devote its time entirely to its programme and the elections in September 1997.
Jagland has said he plans no shift of economic or other policy. But newspapers said he could make major cabinet changes to stamp his mark on the government.
Industry and Energy Minister Jens Stoltenberg, a popular member of the Brundtland cabinet, may succeed Sigbjoern Johnsen as finance minister, the financial daily Dagens Naeringsliv said.
Johnsen, who has been sharply criticised by industry leaders and the opposition on a number of issues, could replace Jagland as parliamentary speaker for the Labour Party, it said.
Commentators said they expected Bjoern Tore Godal to stay on as foreign minister but several other portfolios to change hands.
Newspapers praised Brundtland, who has been in office for a total of 10 years and is known internationally for efficient leadership and strong-minded views.

The announcement that she would quit led to speculation that she would seek a top job at the United Nations, possibly aiming to succeed Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali. But she was evasive about her plans.
"She has been an outstanding leader of the government," Aftenposten said in an editorial describing Brundtland's decision to stand down as the end of an era in Norwegian post-war politics.
But it said she had been lucky to lead a country in the middle of an oil bonanza.
Norway, with a population of just 4.3 million, is the world's second-largest oil exporter, after Saudi Arabia, and one of the richest countries in Europe.
"No government has ever had such economic room for manouevre," Aftenposten said.
Tabloid VG said: "Thorbjoern Jagland meets a formidable challenge when he becomes prime minister tomorrow... Gro leaves a vacuum so big that nobody can fill it immediately."
